What time it is, and waiting for it to be later.

**Its own module, and it did not start as one.** `Clock` lived in
`std::env` because both answer "what did the outside world hand this
process", and that grouping cost something the moment anything else wanted
a clock: `env_native.kh` is native-only for `getenv` and `argv`, so the
clock was native-only too -- not because clocks are unportable, but because
of the file it was in. A Worker has `Date.now`. Splitting the two leaves one
small file with one reason to carry `_native`, and a `clock_wasm.kh` is
then an afternoon rather than an untangling.

It also puts the clock where the things that *need* one can import it:
`std::resilience` backs off, and every future timeout and deadline is the
same dependency. Importing `std::env` to get a clock was a line nobody
could explain.

The C side is not ISO C, and that is why these are runtime exports rather
than `extern` bindings to libc. Milliseconds are
`GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` on Windows and `clock_gettime` on Unix -- two
calls, two epochs, two headers -- and ISO C's `time` is whole seconds with
nothing finer spelled the same everywhere. The runtime already knows which
target it was built for.

## Effects

### Clock

```khora
pub effect Clock {
  unix_seconds: () -> Int,
  unix_millis: () -> Int,
  monotonic_millis: () -> Int,
  sleep: (Int) -> (),
}
```

What time it is.

A capability rather than plain functions, and separate from `Env` because
it is a different thing to deny: a library that may read a configuration
variable is not thereby a library that may know how long something took,
and a test that pins one usually wants to pin the other differently.

**Two clocks, not one, and the split is not a detail.** A wall clock says
what time it is and can jump: NTP steps it, an administrator sets it, a
virtual machine resumes with a stale one -- and it can jump *backwards*, so
subtracting two readings of it is not a duration, it is a guess. A
monotonic clock cannot go backwards and is what "how long did this take"
actually wants; its zero is arbitrary, so it can never be a timestamp.

One `millis` would therefore have been the wrong one about half the time,
and the half it was wrong for would be the half that only fails in
production, at 2am, when the clock is stepped an hour. Naming both makes
the caller say which they meant.

#### real

```khora
pub fn real() -> Clock
```

The real clock.

Seconds are milliseconds divided down rather than a second call to ISO C's
`time`, so that a program reading both never sees them straddle a tick.
